subject: Yu et al. (2009)
object: Yu et al. (2009) described a 5-generation Chinese family with isolated (simple) microphthalmia inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. There were 9 affected members aged 6 to 66 years. All had bilateral hyperopia ranging from +4.50 to +11.50 diopters (mean +8.00) and short axial length of 18.22 to 20.26 mm (mean 19.29 mm). Best corrected visual acuity was less than 0.5 in most eyes, and no family member had any other physical anomaly.

subject: Yu et al. (2009)
object: In this family, Yu et al. (2009) reported angle-closure glaucoma or occludable anterior chamber angles in 3 patients, all older than 50 years. The glaucoma was treated by trabeculectomy but kept progressing, and 2 patients eventually developed atrophia bulbi despite repeated surgeries. The authors also noted learning disabilities in one-third of the cases.

subject: Yu et al. (2009)
object: On histologic examination of sclera from affected members, Yu et al. (2009) found diffusely swollen collagen fibers that were twisted or frayed and mixed with normal fibers. In the 2 atrophied globes, collagen alignment was disrupted, the sclera contained coil-like amorphous material and was 3 times normal thickness, and the cornea was also thickened.

subject: Yu et al. (2009)
object: In this Chinese family, Yu et al. (2009) found that the karyotype of all affected members was normal. Two-point linkage analysis with 23 microsatellite markers produced LOD scores below 1 for every marker, which excluded linkage to CHX10, PAX6, MFRP and to the loci on 14q32, 11p and 2q11-q14. The authors predicted that a novel locus was responsible.

subject: Yu et al. (2009)
object: Yu et al. (2009) concluded that excluding all known loci in this autosomal dominant family suggested high genetic heterogeneity in microphthalmia.

subject: Hu et al. (2011)
object: Hu et al. (2011) studied a Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital simple microphthalmia.

subject: Hu et al. (2011)
object: In a Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital simple microphthalmia, Hu et al. (2011) excluded previously reported microphthalmia loci and performed a genomewide scan with 382 microsatellite markers, then fine mapping. They found the highest linkage at D17S1824 (maximum lod score of 4.97 at theta = 0.00). Haplotype analysis placed the disease gene in a 21.57-cM interval between D17S900 and D17S1872 on chromosome 17p12-q12.

subject: Hu et al. (2011)
object: Hu et al. (2011) used PCR and direct sequencing to screen 14 candidate genes in the linked 17p12-q12 region, including CRYBA1 and NCOR1. They also used genomewide SNP genotyping to look for copy number variation. They found no mutation or CNV that accounted for the microphthalmia in the family.

subject: Awadalla et al. (2014)
object: Awadalla et al. (2014) studied a large white family (NNO-SA1) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. The family was recruited in South Australia. Nanophthalmos was defined as an axial length less than 20.0 mm and/or a refractive error greater than +7.00. Of 35 available family members, 16 (46%) had nanophthalmos, with a mean refraction of +11.8 D and a mean axial length of 17.6 mm.

subject: Awadalla et al. (2014)
object: In family NNO-SA1, Awadalla et al. (2014) ran a genome-wide linkage scan with a 10K SNP array. They found significant linkage on chromosome 17 (17p12-q12) between SNP markers rs2323659 and rs967293, with a maximum location score of 4.1.

subject: Awadalla et al. (2014)
object: In affected members of family NNO-SA1, Awadalla et al. (2014) used exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous missense variant, c.577G>C (p.Ala193Pro), in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene. It was the only novel segregating variant within the linked region. The variant was absent from the Exome Variant Server and from 285 local white controls. The authors concluded that TMEM98 most likely causes the disease in this family.

subject: Awadalla et al. (2014)
object: Using RT-PCR, Awadalla et al. (2014) found that TMEM98 was expressed in all ocular tissues tested, including the sclera and the optic nerve head.

subject: Khorram et al. (2015)
object: Khorram et al. (2015) studied a Caucasian family of German heritage living in the United States (pedigree 991-F) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos spanning at least 4 generations. Six of 10 examined members had nanophthalmos, and 3 more were affected by family history report. Affected members had a mean axial eye length of 17.1 +/- 0.31 mm and high hyperopia, with spherical equivalent refractions of +13.0 +/- 0.89 diopters. Unaffected members had +0.71 +/- 0.81 diopters.

subject: Khorram et al. (2015)
object: Khorram et al. (2015) described a Pacific Islander family of Micronesian heritage from the Mariana Islands (pedigree 951-N) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Eight of 10 examined members were affected, and 3 more were affected by family history report. Affected members had a mean axial eye length of 17.4 +/- 0.94 mm, compared with 22.7 +/- 0.38 mm in unaffected members, and hyperopia of +3.93 +/- 1.57 diopters. Axial lengths across both families ranged from 15.9 to 18.4 mm.

subject: Khorram et al. (2015)
object: Khorram et al. (2015) carried out linkage analysis with 6,020 SNPs. In pedigree 991-F, a 20.2-Mb segment of chromosome 17p12-q12 between SNPs rs530664 and rs16523 cosegregated with nanophthalmos. In pedigree 951-N, an overlapping 19.7-Mb region between rs917541 and rs16523 cosegregated with the disease. The authors noted that this region overlapped the locus previously linked to nanophthalmos in a Chinese pedigree.

subject: Khorram et al. (2015)
object: Exome sequencing of an affected member of the US pedigree 991-F found 4 nonsynonymous variants in the linked chromosome 17 region. Khorram et al. (2015) reported that only the heterozygous His196Pro missense mutation in TMEM98 cosegregated with nanophthalmos and was predicted to be pathogenic by SIFT, PolyPhen, and BLOSUM62. The mutation affects a highly conserved histidine and was absent from the Exome Variant Server and 1000 Genomes Project databases.

subject: Khorram et al. (2015)
object: In the Mariana Islands pedigree 951-N, Khorram et al. (2015) used Sanger sequencing to identify a heterozygous 34-bp deletion in TMEM98 (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg) in all 11 affected members tested. The deletion spans the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4, eliminates a splice site, and results in premature termination of translation. It was absent from healthy family members and from public databases.
